Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- China's giant pandas are believed to be safe after Monday's earthquake, but concern is growing over how they will get their next meals. Questions remain about whether infrastructure damage will harm the giant pandas' supply of bamboo. Authorities confirmed Tuesday that captive animals in two of China's major panda reserves were alive, according to Xinhua, China's official news agency. The Wolong Giant Panda Reserve Center in southwest Sichuan province is home to about 86 giant pandas, who were reported safe Tuesday. Staff and critters at neighboring Chengdu Panda Breeding and Research Center were also reported safe, according to a spokesperson for the Atlanta Zoo, which has two pandas on loan from the wildlife reserve. Concern arose in the international wildlife community over damage to the animals' habitat, as authorities continued assessing the scope of damage in the Sichuan province. The mountainous, densely wooded region is the natural habitat for most of the 1,200 giant pandas living in the wild, making it an obvious location for research bases like Wolong and Chengdu. Giant pandas roam the forest in "open cages" that are meant to provide them with a safe, natural environment that will prepare them for release. With the safety of the pandas confirmed, the animals' caregivers are left to determine how resources like food and medical supplies will reach the bases, which contain breeding facilities and triage centers. Bamboo, the pandas' primary source of food, is a major agricultural product in the region, but whether it can be supplied to the pandas despite infrastructure damage is open to question. "Wolong is hard to access under normal conditions, so the heavy road damage makes it even harder," said Kerry Zobor, spokeswoman for the World Wildlife Fund. Zobor said the WWF had confirmed the safety of staff members based in Beijing but had not received word on the conditions in Wolong. She said the WWF was also concerned about members who had been touring the country when the earthquake struck. The group has not been located. Scientists in the United States are hopeful that Chinese researchers will adapt to the situation facing them. David Wildt with the Smithsonian's National Zoological Park in Washington says scientists in Wolong have overcome threats to the giant panda population before. In the late 1990s, the captive giant panda population was in decline, with more animals dying than were born, Wildt said. Thanks to a collaborative effort with American scientists, the Wolong staff was able to reverse the trend. "Our Chinese colleagues are very perceptive when it comes to addressing problems," said Wildt, who has visited Wolong many times as part of the Smithsonian's affiliation with the research base. "Because of their efforts, the population is on the rise today." Wildt said that Chinese scientists have also addressed the issue of alternative food sources. "Artificial diets in the form of protein biscuits have been created for giant pandas. They're not a complete substitute, but they meet the needs of a basic high-fiber diet," said Wildt, who has worked with two pandas that the Smithsonian has on loan from Wolong. "Right now, we're mostly concerned about the staff. If the staff is fine, then the animals will be fine," Wildt said.

"The immediate danger to individual animals is one thing, but our deeper concern is the long-term fragmentation of habitat," said a WWF spokesperson involved in the assessment. ---

**CHENGDU, China** — A magnitude 6.2 earthquake struck the mountainous regions of western Sichuan Province early Tuesday, damaging infrastructure and raising concerns among conservationists about potential disruptions to the bamboo forests that sustain the region's famous giant panda population.

The quake, centered near the edge of a nature reserve in the Qionglai Mountains, triggered landslides that officials say may have affected sections of the bamboo groves critical to both wild and captive pandas.

## Assessing the Damage

Preliminary surveys by the Sichuan Forestry and Grassland Administration indicate that several hillsides experienced significant erosion, though the full extent of damage to bamboo stands remains under evaluation.

"Landslides can bury or uproot entire sections of bamboo forest," said Dr. Li Wei, a wildlife ecologist affiliated with a regional conservation institute. "The immediate concern is not just the loss of standing bamboo, but the disruption to the soil and root systems that bamboo needs to regenerate."

Giant pandas depend on bamboo for roughly 99% of their diet, consuming between 26 and 84 pounds daily. This near-total reliance makes them particularly vulnerable to any disturbance in their food supply.

## Why Bamboo Is So Critical

Unlike many animals, pandas have a limited natural range and specialized dietary needs. Their populations tend to cluster around specific bamboo species that flower and die on cyclical schedules, sometimes leaving pandas temporarily without adequate food even under normal conditions.

"Pandas are essentially specialists living on a generalist's digestive system," explained Dr. Sarah Chen, a conservation biologist who has studied panda feeding behavior. "They evolved from carnivorous ancestors but shifted almost entirely to bamboo. Their guts aren't ideally suited to digest it, which is why they must eat such enormous quantities. Any interruption in supply forces them to travel farther, expending energy they can't easily replace."

## Exploring Alternative Food Sources

In response to the earthquake, conservation authorities have begun evaluating contingency plans, including the transport of bamboo from unaffected regions to supplementary feeding stations.

Experts, however, caution that alternatives are complicated.

"You can't simply swap one bamboo species for another," Dr. Chen noted. "Pandas can be surprisingly picky. In captive settings, we've seen individuals reject unfamiliar bamboo varieties even when hungry. There's a strong learned component to their feeding preferences."

For captive pandas, keepers sometimes supplement diets with specially formulated "panda cakes"—nutrient-dense biscuits made from ingredients like corn, soybeans, and rice, fortified with vitamins and minerals.

"Supplementary feeds can bridge short-term gaps," said Dr. Li. "But they aren't a substitute for a healthy bamboo forest. For wild pandas especially, our best strategy is habitat restoration—replanting bamboo, stabilizing slopes, and maintaining the corridors that let animals move between feeding areas."

## Long-Term Conservation Implications

Conservationists point out that giant pandas have made a notable recovery in recent decades, with the species reclassified from "endangered" to "vulnerable" in 2016. That progress, experts warn, depends on continued protection of their fragmented habitat.

"Events like this earthquake remind us how fragile these gains can be," Dr. Chen said. "Habitat connectivity is the key. When a disaster strikes one area, pandas need to be able to reach another. Fragmented forests turn local disruptions into serious crises."

Authorities emphasized that no panda casualties have been reported, and captive facilities in the region were not significantly damaged. Teams are continuing to monitor wild populations and assess bamboo conditions in the coming weeks.

## What Comes Next

Local and national agencies have pledged resources for habitat recovery, including reforestation efforts and slope stabilization to prevent further landslides during the coming rainy season.

"The pandas are resilient, and so are the forests," Dr. Li said. "With careful management, both can recover. But it requires sustained commitment—not just in the aftermath of a disaster, but for years to come."
